Understanding AI data-center power infrastructure, from the grid to the rack.

AI Power Lab is built from public engineering and industry sources to develop systems-level reasoning and architecture judgment about how AI data centers are actually powered — the equipment, the architecture trade-offs, how the chain behaves under real events, and what is happening in the industry around it.

2Architecture Choices

Why these designs, and what are the trade-offs?

How Conventional AC, AC-fed 800 VDC, and a Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC architecture via solid-state transformer (one optional way to do the grid-side conversion, not a requirement for 800 VDC) compare against illustrative requirement drivers, and what interfaces and validation each would need.

3Learn by Example

4Industry & Career
PLANNED

What's happening in industry, and what does it mean for me?

Public company, product, and standards developments in AI data-center power, tracked over time, framed for an engineer building a systems-architecture career path.

Each area has a different job: the map shows structure, Architecture Choices evaluates alternatives against requirements, Learn by Example explains cause and effect step by step, and Industry & Career connects the knowledge to real-world industry. The Advanced Sandbox is a supporting tool for free quantitative experiments, not a fifth area of equal standing.

What this is, and isn’t

This project uses only public engineering principles, standards, and industry sources — textbooks, published papers, datasheets, and public company/standards disclosures. It is not a commercial product, a research-grade digital twin, or a source of proprietary information from any employer. The underlying simulation (grid → SST → 800 VDC bus → AI load) is a deliberately simple, lumped-parameter, system-level model of one conceptual, emerging architecture, built to teach how the chain behaves — not to reproduce a specific vendor’s hardware or to imply that this architecture is widely deployed.

WHAT IT IS

WHY IT EXISTS, CONSIDERATIONS & ALTERNATIVES
Thirty seconds on what this is
What is an SST?
A power-electronic converter that performs voltage transformation (and often AC/DC conversion) using active semiconductor switching and a medium-frequency transformer, instead of a passive line-frequency transformer. It is one candidate for the medium-voltage-to-DC stage, proposed to reduce the number of conversion stages; it is not required for 800 VDC (Architecture Choices compares the options).
Why does 800 VDC matter?
Public industry sources (NVIDIA, the Open Compute Project) describe an industry shift toward centralized power conversion and an 800 VDC distribution bus for high-density AI racks, aiming to cut the number of conversion stages between the grid and the compute load.
Why do AI data centers create new power challenges?
AI compute workloads can swing power demand fast and hard -- the Advanced Sandbox (linked at the end of this page) runs this project's AI load-step scenario, showing that kind of transient and how the model responds to it.
What does this project simulate?
The full causal chain Grid → SST (average-value model) → 800 VDC bus → AI load, including a PI voltage controller, a lumped thermal model, and thermal-driven protection/derating -- run it in the Advanced Sandbox (linked at the end of this page).
What does it NOT simulate yet?
No switching-level semiconductor behavior, no detailed SiC/GaN device physics, no medium-frequency-transformer electromagnetics, no AC power flow -- the SST is one aggregate average-value block. The Advanced Sandbox (linked at the end of this page) shows the live model.
What this project actually simulates

The map above is a broad infrastructure overview. This project’s live simulation (the Advanced Sandbox) models one narrow, specific slice of it: the grid → SST → 800 VDC bus → AI compute chain, drawn below exactly as the simulator draws it -- an instance of the Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST architecture view above, not a fourth, separate topology.

WHY THIS HAPPENED

At t = 0.20 s, AI demand jumps almost instantly — far faster than this model’s SST (solid-state transformer) response time constant lets delivered power follow. While demand outruns delivery, the DC bus supplies the missing power from its own stored energy, and V_dc falls as that energy drains — reaching a minimum of 712.5 V. To close the gap, the controller doesn’t just raise SST power to match demand — it pushes SST power above demand for a while, which is what actually refills the bus’s stored energy and drives V_dc back up toward the 800 V reference; once the bus is recharged, SST power settles back down to match demand again.

How far V_dc sags is set by the accumulated energy deficit — the area under the power-mismatch curve while demand outruns delivery — not by how tall that gap’s peak is: a tall but brief mismatch drains little; a modest one that lasts drains more. Here that works out to 1.3 kJ drawn from the DC link (the shaded area on the Power Balance chart below; every other number this derivation uses is in ENGINEERING RESULT, further down).

SHOW ALL SEVEN DRIVERS, COMPARISONS AND DECISIONS
Rack power and growth

How much power must reach each rack, and how does delivery scale as that grows?

What it is

The power each rack draws, and the path by which that power is expected to increase.

Why it matters

AI compute concentrates power in each rack, so delivery equipment must be sized for rack power and for its growth.

System connection

Sets current, conductor and conversion capacity from the distribution stage to the rack input.

Constraints and trade-offs

Higher delivery capacity costs equipment, space and money; unused headroom is stranded capacity.

Decision it informs

Which distribution voltage and form to build for the expected range of rack power.

2Compare architectures

How does each architecture meet this driver?

Qualitative only. “Harder” is what the architecture makes more difficult for that driver, not a score. SST is one candidate technology for the medium-voltage-to-DC stage. It is not required for 800 VDC: the AC-fed 800 VDC architecture reaches the same bus without one.

Rack power and growth
Conventional AC
How it is addressed

Rack power is delivered as AC at a chosen distribution voltage. For a given voltage, conductor arrangement and power factor, more rack power means proportionally more current, so growth is met with larger conductors or more circuits. The OCP article describes the baseline as medium-voltage AC stepped down to 480 VAC feeding AC racks.

What it makes harder

Large steps in rack power push conductor and busway size, or the number of circuits, upward.

PUBLIC FACT — Power–current relation (textbook principle; reference not inspected); OCP article's description of the baseline architecture.
Refs: GRAINGER (textbook/standard, background), OCP (consortium document), SYSMAP (this site)

AC-fed 800 VDC
How it is addressed

For the same power, a higher distribution voltage means lower current per conductor, all else equal. The actual benefit depends on the AC voltage and phase arrangement it is compared with and on the DC conductor arrangement; the OCP white paper's wiring analysis (§6.3.3) shows that, for a given power, moving to a higher voltage class with correspondingly less conductor material can reduce relative cable losses and current, and that a bipolar arrangement with a midpoint conductor can reduce losses compared with a unipolar one when loads are balanced. Both NVIDIA and the OCP white paper cite rising rack power density as the motivation for DC distribution.

What it makes harder

It needs rack-level DC-DC conversion and DC-rated equipment that conventional racks do not use.

PUBLIC FACT — Power–current relation (textbook principle; reference not inspected); OCP white paper executive summary and §6.3.3 wiring analysis; NVIDIA vendor statement on rack density.
Refs: GRAINGER (textbook/standard, background), OCPWP (consortium document), NVIDIA (vendor statement), SYSMAP (this site)

Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST
How it is addressed

The distribution-voltage benefit is the same as AC-fed 800 VDC. The difference is upstream, where an SST is the conceptual medium-voltage-to-DC source.

What it makes harder

Supplying a facility-scale DC block this way depends on SST technology that is still being specified: NVIDIA describes direct medium-voltage conversion only for a future facility-scale unit, and the OCP SST specification is a first draft (Rev 0.3.0) with open items.

EMERGING / UNCERTAIN — NVIDIA vendor statement on a future facility-scale DC power block; OCP SST specification version history and TBD items.
Refs: NVIDIA (vendor statement), OCPSST (consortium document)

The Advanced Sandbox simulates only the Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST slice, as a simplified average-value model. It does not validate, size or benchmark Conventional AC or AC-fed 800 VDC, and it is not evidence that any architecture is better.

A conditional tendency with its exceptions, not a verdict. This page does not rank architectures or name a winner; every conditional statement depends on which driver dominates for a given site.

WHY THIS HAPPENED

At t = 0.20 s, AI demand jumps almost instantly — far faster than this model’s SST (solid-state transformer) response time constant lets delivered power follow. While demand outruns delivery, the DC bus supplies the missing power from its own stored energy, and V_dc falls as that energy drains — reaching a minimum of 712.5 V. To close the gap, the controller doesn’t just raise SST power to match demand — it pushes SST power above demand for a while, which is what actually refills the bus’s stored energy and drives V_dc back up toward the 800 V reference; once the bus is recharged, SST power settles back down to match demand again.

How far V_dc sags is set by the accumulated energy deficit — the area under the power-mismatch curve while demand outruns delivery — not by how tall that gap’s peak is: a tall but brief mismatch drains little; a modest one that lasts drains more. Here that works out to 1.3 kJ drawn from the DC link (the shaded area on the Power Balance chart below; every other number this derivation uses is in ENGINEERING RESULT, further down).

Tends to favor

AC-fed 800 VDC · Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST

Because

At a higher distribution voltage the same power needs lower current per conductor, all else equal, which can ease conductor sizing as rack power grows; the benefit depends on the AC voltage and conductor arrangement being compared.

·
Standards and equipment maturity must be settled before commitment (see standards and ecosystem maturity).

EVALUATE ALTERNATIVES AGAINST REQUIREMENTS

Architecture choices

Three architectures from the System Map — Conventional AC, AC-fed 800 VDC, Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST — are compared against seven requirement drivers. The aim is to practice reasoning from requirements to an architecture choice, and to name what must be validated before relying on it.

Next: Learn by Example: see how the system behaves under a disturbance

Basis and limits
SST
SST is one candidate technology for the medium-voltage-to-DC stage. It is not required for 800 VDC: the AC-fed 800 VDC architecture reaches the same bus without one.
BLOCKS
Blocks in these architectures are functional abstractions, not literal single-stage converters or literal racks; real equipment is internally multi-stage.
SIMULATION
The Advanced Sandbox simulates only the Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST slice, as a simplified average-value model. It does not validate, size or benchmark Conventional AC or AC-fed 800 VDC, and it is not evidence that any architecture is better.
DRIVERS
Requirement drivers are illustrative teaching assumptions, not a design basis for any facility.
NO WINNER
This page does not rank architectures or name a winner; every conditional statement depends on which driver dominates for a given site.

Each item carries an evidence label: Public fact (principle or attributed source), Illustrative assumption, Model output (simplified), or Emerging / uncertain. An item carries the label of its weakest claim.

BACK TO THE SELECTED DRIVER
Rack power and growth

How much power must reach each rack, and how does delivery scale as that grows?

What it is

The power each rack draws, and the path by which that power is expected to increase.

Why it matters

AI compute concentrates power in each rack, so delivery equipment must be sized for rack power and for its growth.

System connection

Sets current, conductor and conversion capacity from the distribution stage to the rack input.

Constraints and trade-offs

Higher delivery capacity costs equipment, space and money; unused headroom is stranded capacity.

Decision it informs

Which distribution voltage and form to build for the expected range of rack power.

Load dynamics

How fast can the load change, and where does the energy buffer sit?

What it is

How quickly rack power can swing and how far the supply side must absorb that swing.

Why it matters

A load step the supply cannot absorb becomes a voltage excursion on the bus or a disturbance seen upstream.

System connection

Couples load behavior to the energy buffer, converter control response and the grid-side interface.

Constraints and trade-offs

More buffering and faster control reduce excursions but add equipment, cost and control complexity.

Decision it informs

Where to place stored energy and how fast the conversion stage must respond.

Availability and maintainability

What redundancy exists, and can a section be isolated and worked on?

What it is

How the design tolerates a failed component and allows maintenance without losing the load.

Why it matters

Compute load lost to a single failure or maintenance action is costly, and redundancy has its own cost.

System connection

Spans switchgear arrangement, conversion modules, storage and generation integration.

Constraints and trade-offs

Higher redundancy (N+1, 2N) adds equipment and footprint; fewer series elements reduce failure points but concentrate risk.

Decision it informs

What redundancy scheme and isolation capability each stage needs.

Safety and protection practice

How are faults cleared, and how is personnel safety managed?

What it is

How fault current is detected and interrupted, and the practice that keeps people safe around energized equipment.

Why it matters

Fault energy and touch hazard depend on voltage, current and clearing time, and practice must match the technology.

System connection

Links distribution voltage and form, protective devices and the monitoring/control system.

Constraints and trade-offs

Faster, more selective protection costs complexity; unfamiliar technology means practice is less settled.

Decision it informs

What protection scheme and safe-work practice the chosen distribution form requires.

Conversion chain and losses

How many series conversion functions exist, and where is heat produced?

What it is

The count of series conversion functions between grid and compute, and the loss each one adds.

Why it matters

Each conversion function dissipates some power as heat, which must be rejected and paid for.

System connection

Connects the conversion stage choice to cooling load and operating cost.

Constraints and trade-offs

Fewer stages can mean lower loss on paper but more stress per stage and different failure modes.

Decision it informs

Whether consolidating conversion functions is worth the new interface and protection requirements.

Physical footprint

What space, conductor cross-section and cooling infrastructure does delivery require?

What it is

The floor space, copper and cooling plant needed to deliver the power.

Why it matters

Space and conductor mass are costly, and more space means longer runs and more loss.

System connection

Ties the distribution voltage to conductor size and the conversion stage to cooling infrastructure.

Constraints and trade-offs

Smaller conductors from higher voltage can be offset by larger or more specialized conversion and cooling equipment.

Decision it informs

How to allocate floor space between conversion equipment, storage, distribution and compute.

Standards and ecosystem maturity

How settled are the standards, equipment supply and operating practice?

What it is

How established the governing standards, supplier base and field experience are.

Why it matters

Unsettled standards risk interoperability gaps, supply constraints and rework.

System connection

Affects every interface, because standards define what must interoperate at each boundary.

Constraints and trade-offs

Mature practice lowers risk but may limit density; emerging practice offers capability with higher uncertainty.

Decision it informs

How much emerging-technology risk the program accepts for the capability it needs.

2Compare architectures

How does each architecture meet this driver?

Qualitative only. “Harder” is what the architecture makes more difficult for that driver, not a score. SST is one candidate technology for the medium-voltage-to-DC stage. It is not required for 800 VDC: the AC-fed 800 VDC architecture reaches the same bus without one.

Rack power and growth
Conventional AC
How it is addressed

Rack power is delivered as AC at a chosen distribution voltage. For a given voltage, conductor arrangement and power factor, more rack power means proportionally more current, so growth is met with larger conductors or more circuits. The OCP article describes the baseline as medium-voltage AC stepped down to 480 VAC feeding AC racks.

What it makes harder

Large steps in rack power push conductor and busway size, or the number of circuits, upward.

PUBLIC FACT — Power–current relation (textbook principle; reference not inspected); OCP article's description of the baseline architecture.
Refs: GRAINGER (textbook/standard, background), OCP (consortium document), SYSMAP (this site)

AC-fed 800 VDC
How it is addressed

For the same power, a higher distribution voltage means lower current per conductor, all else equal. The actual benefit depends on the AC voltage and phase arrangement it is compared with and on the DC conductor arrangement; the OCP white paper's wiring analysis (§6.3.3) shows that, for a given power, moving to a higher voltage class with correspondingly less conductor material can reduce relative cable losses and current, and that a bipolar arrangement with a midpoint conductor can reduce losses compared with a unipolar one when loads are balanced. Both NVIDIA and the OCP white paper cite rising rack power density as the motivation for DC distribution.

What it makes harder

It needs rack-level DC-DC conversion and DC-rated equipment that conventional racks do not use.

PUBLIC FACT — Power–current relation (textbook principle; reference not inspected); OCP white paper executive summary and §6.3.3 wiring analysis; NVIDIA vendor statement on rack density.
Refs: GRAINGER (textbook/standard, background), OCPWP (consortium document), NVIDIA (vendor statement), SYSMAP (this site)

Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST
How it is addressed

The distribution-voltage benefit is the same as AC-fed 800 VDC. The difference is upstream, where an SST is the conceptual medium-voltage-to-DC source.

What it makes harder

Supplying a facility-scale DC block this way depends on SST technology that is still being specified: NVIDIA describes direct medium-voltage conversion only for a future facility-scale unit, and the OCP SST specification is a first draft (Rev 0.3.0) with open items.

EMERGING / UNCERTAIN — NVIDIA vendor statement on a future facility-scale DC power block; OCP SST specification version history and TBD items.
Refs: NVIDIA (vendor statement), OCPSST (consortium document)

Load dynamics
Conventional AC
How it is addressed

A double-conversion UPS places a DC link and battery between the AC source and the load, which can decouple load swings from the upstream source. How much depends on the UPS design.

What it makes harder

Fast swings must still be absorbed within the UPS inverter and DC link ratings; this page gives no ratings.

PUBLIC FACT — Double-conversion UPS topology (textbook principle; reference not inspected); System Map description.
Refs: MOHAN (textbook/standard, background), SYSMAP (this site)

AC-fed 800 VDC
How it is addressed

Storage attaches directly to the DC bus. Bus capacitance and the control of the centralized AC-DC stage set how far voltage moves in a load step (stored capacitor energy is ½CV², a relation also exercised in this repository's DC-bus tests). The OCP white paper examines closer integration of energy storage as part of DC distribution.

What it makes harder

Bus voltage regulation becomes a control interface between the centralized stage and the rack DC-DC converters.

PUBLIC FACT — Capacitor energy relation (principle); OCP white paper efficiency discussion; System Map description of storage on the DC bus.
Refs: MOHAN (textbook/standard, background), OCPWP (consortium document), SYSMAP (this site)

Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST
How it is addressed

The DC-bus mechanics match AC-fed 800 VDC, with the SST's control response also in the loop. The Advanced Sandbox illustrates this slice with a simplified model: an AI load step produces a bus-voltage sag whose size depends on bus capacitance and SST response time.

What it makes harder

A fast load step also stresses the grid side of the SST. The Sandbox's simplified model does not represent real SST internals and validates no product.

MODEL OUTPUT (SIMPLIFIED) — Calculated by the simplified Sandbox model from stated educational assumptions; applies to this slice only.
Refs: SANDBOX (this site)

Availability and maintainability
Conventional AC
How it is addressed

The OCP white paper cites strategies such as N+1 power blocks and UPS maintenance bypass for managing power-electronics failures, and the System Map describes N+1 and 2N redundancy.

What it makes harder

More series equipment (transformers, UPS plant, distribution) has to be maintained.

PUBLIC FACT — OCP white paper redundancy section; System Map redundancy discussion; commercial power-system reliability practice (textbook; reference not inspected).
Refs: OCPWP (consortium document), GOLDBOOK (textbook/standard, background), SYSMAP (this site)

AC-fed 800 VDC
How it is addressed

Redundancy concepts such as N+1 can be applied to centralized conversion modules and the DC bus, but the OCP white paper says DC distribution does not allow a UPS maintenance-bypass strategy, so redundancy is needed at power-block level and possibly in distribution.

What it makes harder

The OCP white paper says strategies for availability in LVDC data centers require further investigation; this page cites no operating data for 800 VDC AI data centers.

EMERGING / UNCERTAIN — OCP white paper section on redundancy levels and availability.
Refs: OCPWP (consortium document), OCP (consortium document)

Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST
How it is addressed

The OCP SST specification illustrates block (catcher) and distributed redundancy arrangements, and the OCP white paper says major building blocks are moving toward modular sub-blocks with live-swap capability.

What it makes harder

Voltage levels for seamless redundancy design are an open (TBD) item in the SST specification, and this page cites no field data for a medium-voltage solid-state stage.

EMERGING / UNCERTAIN — OCP SST specification Appendix A and TBD items; OCP white paper availability discussion.
Refs: OCPSST (consortium document), OCPWP (consortium document)

Safety and protection practice
Conventional AC
How it is addressed

Installation practice and protective devices for AC are codified (the OCP white paper cites NFPA 70 and IEC 60364), and AC selectivity by time-current settings is the most widespread method. AC current's periodic zero crossings assist arc interruption (textbook principle; reference not inspected).

What it makes harder

Arc-flash incident energy depends on fault current and protective clearing time together; the OCP white paper notes that time-current selectivity delays in AC systems can mean long arcing time in an arc flash. It must be reassessed whenever capacity or configuration changes.

PUBLIC FACT — OCP white paper protection section; NFPA 70, IEC 60364 and IEEE 1584 as general background (not inspected).
Refs: OCPWP (consortium document), NEC (textbook/standard, background), IEEE1584 (textbook/standard, background), GARZON (textbook/standard, background)

AC-fed 800 VDC
How it is addressed

DC interruption needs devices rated for DC. The OCP white paper describes conventional fuses and breakers interrupting by creating an arc voltage above the system voltage, and newer semiconductor-based devices. Clearances and personnel practice for 800 V DC differ from AC practice.

What it makes harder

The OCP white paper states there is currently no standard or recognized practice for coordinating protection for the DC fault behaviors it describes, and no DC equivalent of IEEE 1584 for incident energy; the OCP article reports engagement with UL Solutions, NFPA, IEEE and IEC.

EMERGING / UNCERTAIN — OCP white paper protection section and incident-energy note; OCP article on standards and safety organizations.
Refs: OCPWP (consortium document), OCP (consortium document)

Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST
How it is addressed

The OCP white paper's converter classification lists galvanic isolation by a high-frequency transformer, and notes fault-limiting converters can hold steady-state fault current to zero or low values.

What it makes harder

The white paper says migrating to solid-state solutions may need a new approach to coordination studies, and the OCP SST specification is a first draft in which short-circuit duration and other values are still TBD.

EMERGING / UNCERTAIN — OCP white paper converter classification and protection discussion; OCP SST specification TBD items.
Refs: OCPWP (consortium document), OCPSST (consortium document)

Conversion chain and losses
Conventional AC
How it is addressed

Power passes through AC-DC-AC conversion in a double-conversion UPS and AC-DC again in rack supplies. Each series function dissipates some power as heat, and series efficiencies multiply. The OCP article describes direct DC architectures as removing intermediate AC conversion stages and repeated AC/DC conversions.

What it makes harder

Repeated conversion compounds losses and heat; this page gives no efficiency figures.

PUBLIC FACT — Series efficiency multiplication (textbook principle; reference not inspected); System Map conversion chain; OCP article.
Refs: MOHAN (textbook/standard, background), SYSMAP (this site), OCP (consortium document)

AC-fed 800 VDC
How it is addressed

A centralized AC-DC stage replaces the UPS AC-AC chain. NVIDIA says 800 VDC leaves fewer conversion stages between grid and accelerator, and the OCP white paper cites a potential reduction in conversion stages while noting that realized gains depend on site-specific design.

What it makes harder

The side-rack option still performs AC-to-DC conversion locally, the net stage count still depends on equipment upstream of the DC bus, and neither NVIDIA nor the OCP article gives a stage count or efficiency figure here, so no efficiency comparison is made.

PUBLIC FACT — NVIDIA vendor statement and OCP white paper efficiency discussion (attributed, not endorsed); OCP article description of the side-rack option.
Refs: NVIDIA (vendor statement), OCPWP (consortium document), OCP (consortium document), SYSMAP (this site)

Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST
How it is addressed

The OCP SST specification defines the SST as replacing the line-frequency medium-voltage transformer, rectifier units and, as required, energy storage: one functional block.

What it makes harder

The specification is a black-box definition that lists several product components (power conversion, MVAC input, LVDC output, firmware and control, auxiliary power) and gives no stage count, so any stage reduction is not shown; general engineering practice is that such a converter is internally multi-stage; the efficiency of any real SST is product-specific and not compared here.

PUBLIC FACT — OCP SST specification scope and product-composition sections; System Map SST caveat.
Refs: OCPSST (consortium document), SYSMAP (this site)

Physical footprint
Conventional AC
How it is addressed

At a given distribution voltage and conductor arrangement, more power means more current and so more conductor cross-section for the same loss; UPS and battery rooms also occupy floor space.

What it makes harder

Footprint grows with UPS plant and conductor size as rack power rises.

PUBLIC FACT — Conductor loss and sizing relations (textbook principle; reference not inspected); System Map UPS and battery plant description.
Refs: GRAINGER (textbook/standard, background), SYSMAP (this site)

AC-fed 800 VDC
How it is addressed

Where the distribution voltage is higher for the same power and loss basis, conductors can be smaller. The saving depends on the comparison basis (AC voltage, phases, power factor, DC arrangement); the OCP white paper examines improved utilization of conductors while noting that realized gains depend on site-specific design. Centralized conversion equipment still needs space and cooling.

What it makes harder

It moves heat and floor space from UPS rooms to conversion blocks and rack DC-DC stages; no sizing is claimed.

PUBLIC FACT — Conductor loss and sizing relations (textbook principle; reference not inspected); OCP white paper efficiency discussion.
Refs: GRAINGER (textbook/standard, background), OCPWP (consortium document)

Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST
How it is addressed

The OCP SST specification states that an SST uses medium-to-high-frequency magnetic components and targets higher power density; smaller magnetics at higher frequency is a textbook relationship.

What it makes harder

Cooling of the power section and packaging of new equipment become design questions; this page makes no footprint comparison.

PUBLIC FACT — OCP SST specification scope statement (a design target, not measured performance); transformer size–frequency relation (textbook; reference not inspected).
Refs: OCPSST (consortium document), MOHAN (textbook/standard, background)

Standards and ecosystem maturity
Conventional AC
How it is addressed

AC distribution is covered by established codes and standards (for example NFPA 70 and IEC 60364, both cited by the OCP white paper) and long operating practice.

What it makes harder

The OCP white paper says rising rack power density and more dynamic loads are pushing data-center power beyond the limits of traditional architectures.

PUBLIC FACT — OCP white paper executive summary; NFPA 70 and IEC 60364 as cited there.
Refs: OCPWP (consortium document), NEC (textbook/standard, background), GOLDBOOK (textbook/standard, background)

AC-fed 800 VDC
How it is addressed

The OCP article describes a Google, Microsoft and NVIDIA workstream to standardize 800 VDC (LVDC) data-center power, including an AC-fed side power rack option and a direct medium-voltage-to-800 VDC option.

What it makes harder

Standards are still being developed: the OCP article describes engagement with UL Solutions, NFPA, IEEE and IEC on certification and regulatory frameworks. Interoperability and equipment availability should be verified, and this page makes no adoption claim.

EMERGING / UNCERTAIN — OCP article description of the standardization workstream and safety-organization engagement.
Refs: OCP (consortium document), NVIDIA (vendor statement)

Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST
How it is addressed

The OCP SST specification (Rev 0.3.0, effective 22 June 2026) defines the SST as a black box, with a focus on electrical, mechanical, thermal, control and communications interfaces.

What it makes harder

Its own version history calls it a first draft and several values are TBD (for example short-circuit fault duration); this page makes no adoption claim and no maturity ordering among the architectures.

EMERGING / UNCERTAIN — OCP SST specification version history, scope and TBD items.
Refs: OCPSST (consortium document)

The Advanced Sandbox simulates only the Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST slice, as a simplified average-value model. It does not validate, size or benchmark Conventional AC or AC-fed 800 VDC, and it is not evidence that any architecture is better.

WHY THIS HAPPENED

At t = 0.20 s, AI demand jumps almost instantly — far faster than this model’s SST (solid-state transformer) response time constant lets delivered power follow. While demand outruns delivery, the DC bus supplies the missing power from its own stored energy, and V_dc falls as that energy drains — reaching a minimum of 712.5 V. To close the gap, the controller doesn’t just raise SST power to match demand — it pushes SST power above demand for a while, which is what actually refills the bus’s stored energy and drives V_dc back up toward the 800 V reference; once the bus is recharged, SST power settles back down to match demand again.

How far V_dc sags is set by the accumulated energy deficit — the area under the power-mismatch curve while demand outruns delivery — not by how tall that gap’s peak is: a tall but brief mismatch drains little; a modest one that lasts drains more. Thirty seconds on what this is
What is an SST?
A power-electronic converter that performs voltage transformation (and often AC/DC conversion) using active semiconductor switching and a medium-frequency transformer, instead of a passive line-frequency transformer. It is one candidate for the medium-voltage-to-DC stage, proposed to reduce the number of conversion stages; it is not required for 800 VDC (Architecture Choices compares the options).
Why does 800 VDC matter?
Public industry sources (NVIDIA, the Open Compute Project) describe an industry shift toward centralized power conversion and an 800 VDC distribution bus for high-density AI racks, aiming to cut the number of conversion stages between the grid and the compute load.
Why do AI data centers create new power challenges?
AI compute workloads can swing power demand fast and hard -- the Advanced Sandbox (linked at the end of this page) runs this project's AI load-step scenario, showing that kind of transient and how the model responds to it.

The full causal chain Grid → SST (average-value model) → 800 VDC bus → AI load, including a PI voltage controller, a lumped thermal model, and thermal-driven protection/derating -- run it in the Advanced Sandbox (linked at the end of this page).

No switching-level semiconductor behavior, no detailed SiC/GaN device physics, no medium-frequency-transformer electromagnetics, no AC power flow -- the SST is one aggregate average-value block. The Advanced Sandbox (linked at the end of this page) shows the live model.

WHY THIS HAPPENED

At t = 0.20 s, AI demand jumps almost instantly — far faster than this model’s SST (solid-state transformer) response time constant lets delivered power follow. While demand outruns delivery, the DC bus supplies the missing power from its own stored energy, and V_dc falls as that energy drains — reaching a minimum of 712.5 V. To close the gap, the controller doesn’t just raise SST power to match demand — it pushes SST power above demand for a while, which is what actually refills the bus’s stored energy and drives V_dc back up toward the 800 V reference; once the bus is recharged, SST power settles back down to match demand again.

How far V_dc sags is set by the accumulated energy deficit — the area under the power-mismatch curve while demand outruns delivery — not by how tall that gap’s peak is: a tall but brief mismatch drains little; a modest one that lasts drains more. How much power must reach each rack, and how does delivery scale as that grows?

What it is

The power each rack draws, and the path by which that power is expected to increase.

Why it matters

AI compute concentrates power in each rack, so delivery equipment must be sized for rack power and for its growth.

System connection

Sets current, conductor and conversion capacity from the distribution stage to the rack input.

Constraints and trade-offs

Higher delivery capacity costs equipment, space and money; unused headroom is stranded capacity.

Decision it informs

Which distribution voltage and form to build for the expected range of rack power.

2Compare architectures

How does each architecture meet this driver?

Qualitative only. “Harder” is what the architecture makes more difficult for that driver, not a score. SST is one candidate technology for the medium-voltage-to-DC stage. It is not required for 800 VDC: the AC-fed 800 VDC architecture reaches the same bus without one.

Rack power and growth
Conventional AC
How it is addressed

Rack power is delivered as AC at a chosen distribution voltage. For a given voltage, conductor arrangement and power factor, more rack power means proportionally more current, so growth is met with larger conductors or more circuits. The OCP article describes the baseline as medium-voltage AC stepped down to 480 VAC feeding AC racks.

What it makes harder

Large steps in rack power push conductor and busway size, or the number of circuits, upward.

PUBLIC FACT — Power–current relation (textbook principle; reference not inspected); OCP article's description of the baseline architecture.
Refs: GRAINGER (textbook/standard, background), OCP (consortium document), SYSMAP (this site)

AC-fed 800 VDC
How it is addressed

For the same power, a higher distribution voltage means lower current per conductor, all else equal. The actual benefit depends on the AC voltage and phase arrangement it is compared with and on the DC conductor arrangement; the OCP white paper's wiring analysis (§6.3.3) shows that, for a given power, moving to a higher voltage class with correspondingly less conductor material can reduce relative cable losses and current, and that a bipolar arrangement with a midpoint conductor can reduce losses compared with a unipolar one when loads are balanced. Both NVIDIA and the OCP white paper cite rising rack power density as the motivation for DC distribution.

What it makes harder

It needs rack-level DC-DC conversion and DC-rated equipment that conventional racks do not use.

PUBLIC FACT — Power–current relation (textbook principle; reference not inspected); OCP white paper executive summary and §6.3.3 wiring analysis; NVIDIA vendor statement on rack density.
Refs: GRAINGER (textbook/standard, background), OCPWP (consortium document), NVIDIA (vendor statement), SYSMAP (this site)

Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST
How it is addressed

The distribution-voltage benefit is the same as AC-fed 800 VDC. The difference is upstream, where an SST is the conceptual medium-voltage-to-DC source.

What it makes harder

Supplying a facility-scale DC block this way depends on SST technology that is still being specified: NVIDIA describes direct medium-voltage conversion only for a future facility-scale unit, and the OCP SST specification is a first draft (Rev 0.3.0) with open items.

EMERGING / UNCERTAIN — NVIDIA vendor statement on a future facility-scale DC power block; OCP SST specification version history and TBD items.
Refs: NVIDIA (vendor statement), OCPSST (consortium document)

The Advanced Sandbox simulates only the Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST slice, as a simplified average-value model. It does not validate, size or benchmark Conventional AC or AC-fed 800 VDC, and it is not evidence that any architecture is better.

WHY THIS HAPPENED

At t = 0.20 s, AI demand jumps almost instantly — far faster than this model’s SST (solid-state transformer) response time constant lets delivered power follow. While demand outruns delivery, the DC bus supplies the missing power from its own stored energy, and V_dc falls as that energy drains — reaching a minimum of 712.5 V. To close the gap, the controller doesn’t just raise SST power to match demand — it pushes SST power above demand for a while, which is what actually refills the bus’s stored energy and drives V_dc back up toward the 800 V reference; once the bus is recharged, SST power settles back down to match demand again.

How far V_dc sags is set by the accumulated energy deficit — the area under the power-mismatch curve while demand outruns delivery — not by how tall that gap’s peak is: a tall but brief mismatch drains little; a modest one that lasts drains more. Here that works out to 1.3 kJ drawn from the DC link (the shaded area on the Power Balance chart below; every other number this derivation uses is in ENGINEERING RESULT, further down).

A load step the supply cannot absorb becomes a voltage excursion on the bus or a disturbance seen upstream.

System connection

Couples load behavior to the energy buffer, converter control response and the grid-side interface.

Constraints and trade-offs

More buffering and faster control reduce excursions but add equipment, cost and control complexity.

Decision it informs

Where to place stored energy and how fast the conversion stage must respond.

Availability and maintainability

What redundancy exists, and can a section be isolated and worked on?

What it is

How the design tolerates a failed component and allows maintenance without losing the load.

Why it matters

Compute load lost to a single failure or maintenance action is costly, and redundancy has its own cost.

System connection

Spans switchgear arrangement, conversion modules, storage and generation integration.

Constraints and trade-offs

Higher redundancy (N+1, 2N) adds equipment and footprint; fewer series elements reduce failure points but concentrate risk.

Decision it informs

What redundancy scheme and isolation capability each stage needs.

Safety and protection practice

How are faults cleared, and how is personnel safety managed?

What it is

How fault current is detected and interrupted, and the practice that keeps people safe around energized equipment.

Why it matters

Fault energy and touch hazard depend on voltage, current and clearing time, and practice must match the technology.

System connection

Links distribution voltage and form, protective devices and the monitoring/control system.

Constraints and trade-offs

Faster, more selective protection costs complexity; unfamiliar technology means practice is less settled.

Decision it informs

What protection scheme and safe-work practice the chosen distribution form requires.

Conversion chain and losses

How many series conversion functions exist, and where is heat produced?

What it is

The count of series conversion functions between grid and compute, and the loss each one adds.

Why it matters

Each conversion function dissipates some power as heat, which must be rejected and paid for.

System connection

Connects the conversion stage choice to cooling load and operating cost.

Constraints and trade-offs

Fewer stages can mean lower loss on paper but more stress per stage and different failure modes.

Decision it informs

Whether consolidating conversion functions is worth the new interface and protection requirements.

Physical footprint

What space, conductor cross-section and cooling infrastructure does delivery require?

What it is

The floor space, copper and cooling plant needed to deliver the power.

Why it matters

Space and conductor mass are costly, and more space means longer runs and more loss.

System connection

Ties the distribution voltage to conductor size and the conversion stage to cooling infrastructure.

Constraints and trade-offs

Smaller conductors from higher voltage can be offset by larger or more specialized conversion and cooling equipment.

Decision it informs

How to allocate floor space between conversion equipment, storage, distribution and compute.

Standards and ecosystem maturity

How settled are the standards, equipment supply and operating practice?

What it is

How established the governing standards, supplier base and field experience are.

Why it matters

Unsettled standards risk interoperability gaps, supply constraints and rework.

System connection

Affects every interface, because standards define what must interoperate at each boundary.

Constraints and trade-offs

Mature practice lowers risk but may limit density; emerging practice offers capability with higher uncertainty.

Decision it informs

How much emerging-technology risk the program accepts for the capability it needs.

2Compare architectures

How does each architecture meet this driver?

Qualitative only. “Harder” is what the architecture makes more difficult for that driver, not a score. SST is one candidate technology for the medium-voltage-to-DC stage. It is not required for 800 VDC: the AC-fed 800 VDC architecture reaches the same bus without one.

Rack power and growth
Conventional AC
How it is addressed

Rack power is delivered as AC at a chosen distribution voltage. For a given voltage, conductor arrangement and power factor, more rack power means proportionally more current, so growth is met with larger conductors or more circuits. The OCP article describes the baseline as medium-voltage AC stepped down to 480 VAC feeding AC racks.

What it makes harder

Large steps in rack power push conductor and busway size, or the number of circuits, upward.

PUBLIC FACT — Power–current relation (textbook principle; reference not inspected); OCP article's description of the baseline architecture.
Refs: GRAINGER (textbook/standard, background), OCP (consortium document), SYSMAP (this site)

AC-fed 800 VDC
How it is addressed

For the same power, a higher distribution voltage means lower current per conductor, all else equal. The actual benefit depends on the AC voltage and phase arrangement it is compared with and on the DC conductor arrangement; the OCP white paper's wiring analysis (§6.3.3) shows that, for a given power, moving to a higher voltage class with correspondingly less conductor material can reduce relative cable losses and current, and that a bipolar arrangement with a midpoint conductor can reduce losses compared with a unipolar one when loads are balanced. Both NVIDIA and the OCP white paper cite rising rack power density as the motivation for DC distribution.

What it makes harder

It needs rack-level DC-DC conversion and DC-rated equipment that conventional racks do not use.

PUBLIC FACT — Power–current relation (textbook principle; reference not inspected); OCP white paper executive summary and §6.3.3 wiring analysis; NVIDIA vendor statement on rack density.
Refs: GRAINGER (textbook/standard, background), OCPWP (consortium document), NVIDIA (vendor statement), SYSMAP (this site)

Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST
How it is addressed

The distribution-voltage benefit is the same as AC-fed 800 VDC. The difference is upstream, where an SST is the conceptual medium-voltage-to-DC source.

What it makes harder

Supplying a facility-scale DC block this way depends on SST technology that is still being specified: NVIDIA describes direct medium-voltage conversion only for a future facility-scale unit, and the OCP SST specification is a first draft (Rev 0.3.0) with open items.

EMERGING / UNCERTAIN — NVIDIA vendor statement on a future facility-scale DC power block; OCP SST specification version history and TBD items.
Refs: NVIDIA (vendor statement), OCPSST (consortium document)

Load dynamics
Conventional AC
How it is addressed

A double-conversion UPS places a DC link and battery between the AC source and the load, which can decouple load swings from the upstream source. How much depends on the UPS design.

What it makes harder

Fast swings must still be absorbed within the UPS inverter and DC link ratings; this page gives no ratings.

PUBLIC FACT — Double-conversion UPS topology (textbook principle; reference not inspected); System Map description.
Refs: MOHAN (textbook/standard, background), SYSMAP (this site)

AC-fed 800 VDC
How it is addressed

Storage attaches directly to the DC bus. Bus capacitance and the control of the centralized AC-DC stage set how far voltage moves in a load step (stored capacitor energy is ½CV², a relation also exercised in this repository's DC-bus tests). The OCP white paper examines closer integration of energy storage as part of DC distribution.

What it makes harder

Bus voltage regulation becomes a control interface between the centralized stage and the rack DC-DC converters.

PUBLIC FACT — Capacitor energy relation (principle); OCP white paper efficiency discussion; System Map description of storage on the DC bus.
Refs: MOHAN (textbook/standard, background), OCPWP (consortium document), SYSMAP (this site)

Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST
How it is addressed

The DC-bus mechanics match AC-fed 800 VDC, with the SST's control response also in the loop. The Advanced Sandbox illustrates this slice with a simplified model: an AI load step produces a bus-voltage sag whose size depends on bus capacitance and SST response time.

What it makes harder

A fast load step also stresses the grid side of the SST. The Sandbox's simplified model does not represent real SST internals and validates no product.

How it is addressed

What it makes harder

Safety and protection practice
Conventional AC
How it is addressed

Installation practice and protective devices for AC are codified (the OCP white paper cites NFPA 70 and IEC 60364), and AC selectivity by time-current settings is the most widespread method. AC current's periodic zero crossings assist arc interruption (textbook principle; reference not inspected).

What it makes harder

Arc-flash incident energy depends on fault current and protective clearing time together; the OCP white paper notes that time-current selectivity delays in AC systems can mean long arcing time in an arc flash. It must be reassessed whenever capacity or configuration changes.

PUBLIC FACT — OCP white paper protection section; NFPA 70, IEC 60364 and IEEE 1584 as general background (not inspected).
Refs: OCPWP (consortium document), NEC (textbook/standard, background), IEEE1584 (textbook/standard, background), GARZON (textbook/standard, background)

AC-fed 800 VDC
How it is addressed

DC interruption needs devices rated for DC. The OCP white paper describes conventional fuses and breakers interrupting by creating an arc voltage above the system voltage, and newer semiconductor-based devices. Clearances and personnel practice for 800 V DC differ from AC practice.

What it makes harder

The OCP white paper states there is currently no standard or recognized practice for coordinating protection for the DC fault behaviors it describes, and no DC equivalent of IEEE 1584 for incident energy; the OCP article reports engagement with UL Solutions, NFPA, IEEE and IEC.

EMERGING / UNCERTAIN — OCP white paper protection section and incident-energy note; OCP article on standards and safety organizations.
Refs: OCPWP (consortium document), OCP (consortium document)

Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST
How it is addressed

The OCP white paper's converter classification lists galvanic isolation by a high-frequency transformer, and notes fault-limiting converters can hold steady-state fault current to zero or low values.

What it makes harder

The white paper says migrating to solid-state solutions may need a new approach to coordination studies, and the OCP SST specification is a first draft in which short-circuit duration and other values are still TBD.

EMERGING / UNCERTAIN — OCP white paper converter classification and protection discussion; OCP SST specification TBD items.
Refs: OCPWP (consortium document), OCPSST (consortium document)

Conversion chain and losses
Conventional AC
How it is addressed

Power passes through AC-DC-AC conversion in a double-conversion UPS and AC-DC again in rack supplies. Each series function dissipates some power as heat, and series efficiencies multiply. The OCP article describes direct DC architectures as removing intermediate AC conversion stages and repeated AC/DC conversions.

What it makes harder

Repeated conversion compounds losses and heat; this page gives no efficiency figures.

PUBLIC FACT — Series efficiency multiplication (textbook principle; reference not inspected); System Map conversion chain; OCP article.
Refs: MOHAN (textbook/standard, background), SYSMAP (this site), OCP (consortium document)

AC-fed 800 VDC
How it is addressed

A centralized AC-DC stage replaces the UPS AC-AC chain. NVIDIA says 800 VDC leaves fewer conversion stages between grid and accelerator, and the OCP white paper cites a potential reduction in conversion stages while noting that realized gains depend on site-specific design.

What it makes harder

The side-rack option still performs AC-to-DC conversion locally, the net stage count still depends on equipment upstream of the DC bus, and neither NVIDIA nor the OCP article gives a stage count or efficiency figure here, so no efficiency comparison is made.

PUBLIC FACT — NVIDIA vendor statement and OCP white paper efficiency discussion (attributed, not endorsed); OCP article description of the side-rack option.
Refs: NVIDIA (vendor statement), OCPWP (consortium document), OCP (consortium document), SYSMAP (this site)

Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST
How it is addressed

The OCP SST specification defines the SST as replacing the line-frequency medium-voltage transformer, rectifier units and, as required, energy storage: one functional block.

What it makes harder

The specification is a black-box definition that lists several product components (power conversion, MVAC input, LVDC output, firmware and control, auxiliary power) and gives no stage count, so any stage reduction is not shown; general engineering practice is that such a converter is internally multi-stage; the efficiency of any real SST is product-specific and not compared here.

PUBLIC FACT — OCP SST specification scope and product-composition sections; System Map SST caveat.
Refs: OCPSST (consortium document), SYSMAP (this site)

Physical footprint
Conventional AC
How it is addressed

At a given distribution voltage and conductor arrangement, more power means more current and so more conductor cross-section for the same loss; UPS and battery rooms also occupy floor space.

What it makes harder

Footprint grows with UPS plant and conductor size as rack power rises.

PUBLIC FACT — Conductor loss and sizing relations (textbook principle; reference not inspected); System Map UPS and battery plant description.

Centralized conversion equipment still needs space and cooling.

It moves heat and floor space from UPS rooms to conversion blocks and rack DC-DC stages; no sizing is claimed.

Conceptual MV-to-800 VDC via SST
How it is addressed

The OCP SST specification states that an SST uses medium-to-high-frequency magnetic components and targets higher power density; smaller magnetics at higher frequency is a textbook relationship.

Refs: OCPSST (consortium document), MOHAN (textbook/standard, background)

WHY THIS HAPPENED

At t = 0.20 s, AI demand jumps almost instantly — far faster than this model’s SST (solid-state transformer) response time constant lets delivered power follow. While demand outruns delivery, the DC bus supplies the missing power from its own stored energy, and V_dc falls as that energy drains — reaching a minimum of 712.5 V. To close the gap, the controller doesn’t just raise SST power to match demand — it pushes SST power above demand for a while, which is what actually refills the bus’s stored energy and drives V_dc back up toward the 800 V reference; once the bus is recharged, SST power settles back down to match demand again.

How far V_dc sags is set by the accumulated energy deficit — the area under the power-mismatch curve while demand outruns delivery — not by how tall that gap’s peak is: a tall but brief mismatch drains little; a modest one that lasts drains more. Here that works out to 1.3 kJ drawn from the DC link (the shaded area on the Power Balance chart below; every other number this derivation uses is in ENGINEERING RESULT, further down).

WHY THIS HAPPENED

At t = 0.20 s, AI demand jumps almost instantly — far faster than this model’s SST (solid-state transformer) response time constant lets delivered power follow. While demand outruns delivery, the DC bus supplies the missing power from its own stored energy, and V_dc falls as that energy drains — reaching a minimum of 712.5 V. To close the gap, the controller doesn’t just raise SST power to match demand — it pushes SST power above demand for a while, which is what actually refills the bus’s stored energy and drives V_dc back up toward the 800 V reference; once the bus is recharged, SST power settles back down to match demand again.

How far V_dc sags is set by the accumulated energy deficit — the area under the power-mismatch curve while demand outruns delivery — not by how tall that gap’s peak is: a tall but brief mismatch drains little; a modest one that lasts drains more. Here that works out to 1.3 kJ drawn from the DC link (the shaded area on the Power Balance chart below; every other number this derivation uses is in ENGINEERING RESULT, further down).
